title: How Alcatraz Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of Alcatraz Island, from Native American use and the Spanish naming in 1775, through its military fortifications and conversion to a federal penitentiary, to daily prison life, notable inmates like Robert Stroud (the Birdman), the 1962-63 escape attempts including Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers, and the 1969-1971 Indian occupation led by Richard Oakes. The episode opens with news on the Occupy Wall Street protests and closes with listener mail about synthesis versus extraction of natural compounds, and a call for autumn treat recipes.

segments.title: Opening banter and housekeeping
segments.summary: Hosts plug their video podcast, Twitter and Facebook, a radio station airing of the show, and two audio books, then briefly discuss Occupy Wall Street and clashes with police in various cities.

segments.title: 1969 Alcatraz occupation
segments.summary: Richard Oakes led a multi-tribal group of about a hundred Native Americans who occupied Alcatraz in November 1969 demanding a cultural center and Indian university. The occupation eroded over time, the government offered to buy the island for nine dollars and forty cents, and it ended after oil tankers collided and the government cut power and services, with a fire and a tragic death of Oakes's stepdaughter.

segments.title: Early history of Alcatraz name and Spanish naming
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the name Alcatraz, possibly derived from a word for pelicans or gannets, and Native American use of the island for eggs. Juan Manuel de Ayala named it in 1775. The island is the top of a mountain, and in 1847 Lieutenant William H. Warner proposed fortifications.

segments.title: Army citadel and military prison
segments.summary: The island's Army citadel guarded San Francisco Bay during the Civil War-era gold rush period. Guns fired only by mistake, and soldiers who deserted were held in the basement. After the 1906 earthquake, civilian prisoners were moved there, and the citadel was torn down in favor of a military prison built in 1912.

segments.title: Transfer to federal penitentiary and lighthouse
segments.summary: J. Edgar Hoover pushed to make Alcatraz a federal penitentiary as a deterrent. Ownership transferred in the early 1930s and the first civilian prisoners arrived in secrecy. The hosts also mention the lighthouse, the first on the West Coast, which was rebuilt in 1909.

segments.title: Alcatraz island landscape and prison design
segments.summary: The island is rocky with few plants, most introduced by construction crews. The prison was built for about 600 inmates but held around 300. Its design included cells within a concrete wall, lever-operated cell doors, metal detectors, and tool-resistant steel. Cells were small, with three concrete walls and a steel-barred fourth wall.

segments.title: D Block, solitary confinement and Robert Stroud
segments.summary: D Block housed the treatment unit for solitary confinement, with dark cells nine through fourteen and a hole-in-the-floor cell. Robert Stroud, the Birdman, spent much of his time in solitary, and the hosts discuss the 1962 film Birdman of Alcatraz, noting Stroud did not keep birds there. Stroud's earlier criminal past is also described.

segments.title: Daily routine, rules, and prison life
segments.summary: Inmates had twenty-minute meals, worked jobs such as laundry and library, and made brooms and brushes sold only to federal agencies. Guards patrolled from the Gun Gallery and carried illegal saps. Silence was strictly enforced, and inmates had one monthly visit with no physical contact. Families lived on the island and the dining room knives were kept on a silhouetted rack.

segments.title: Alcatraz escape attempts and inmates
segments.summary: Early escape attempts included a man shot on the fence, two prisoners who likely drowned, and Henry Young's attempt with others, after which McCain and Young were recaptured. Al Capone was held there. The hosts note inmates were not all violent criminals, and that Murder in the First is highly fictionalized.

segments.title: 1962 escape by Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers
segments.summary: Frank Morris and brothers Clarence and John Anglin dug through their cell walls over years, used paper-mache heads and a raft made of raincoats, and escaped in 1962. Their bodies were never found. A 2013 National Geographic special and US Marshals reopened the case, and MythBusters tested the escape. The hosts also compare the 1979 FBI closure and the later evidence.

segments.title: Closure of Alcatraz and other island prisons
segments.summary: The escape and physical deterioration led to Alcatraz's closure. The hosts list other island prisons, including Robben Island, Port Arthur, Rikers Island, and Boss Toy in Norway, which has no bars or armed guards and a small grocery store.

segments.title: Listener mail on synthesis versus extraction
segments.summary: A listener named Evan, an undergraduate chemistry student, explains that extracting compounds from plants is often harder than synthesizing them because of separation issues, and that synthetic and extracted products show no chemical difference.

segments.title: Autumn treats call and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss responses to a call for autumn treat recipes and invite listeners to email them, then promote the Stuff from the Future video podcast.
